subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Prosocial Spending
description: A quick, practical guide to Prosocial Spending.

hook.text: People given $20 to spend on others reported more happiness than those told to spend it on themselves.

buildup.text: Dunn's research across 130 countries found that prosocial spending — giving to others — consistently boosts wellbeing.

discovery.text: The effect is stronger when giving feels voluntary, connected to someone, and you can see the impact of your generosity.

twist.text: The joy of giving diminishes if it's obligatory. Forced donations or guilt-driven charity don't produce the same.

climax.text: Set a small recurring amount for giving. Pick causes you care about. The happiness compounds.

punchline.text: Spend on others. It's the best investment in happiness.

quiz.question: What makes prosocial spending increase happiness?
options: Voluntary giving with visible impact boosts wellbeing
Mandatory giving produces the strongest effect

details.summary: Spending money on others through gifts, charity, or treating friends produces greater and longer-lasting happiness than spending the same amount on yourself. This prosocial spending effect appears across cultures and income levels studied worldwide.
details.whyItMatters: The prosocial spending finding overturns the assumption that selfish spending maximizes personal happiness. It suggests that generosity is not just morally good but psychologically optimal for the giver's own wellbeing.
takeaways: Giving money to others increases the giver's happiness more than self-spending
The prosocial spending effect is consistent across cultures and income levels
Even small gifts produce measurable improvements in mood and satisfaction

faq.question: Why does spending on others make us happier than spending on ourselves?
faq.answer: Prosocial spending strengthens social connections, creates feelings of competence and agency, and satisfies the fundamental human need for belonging. Self-spending triggers hedonic adaptation quickly, while the social bonds from giving provide lasting satisfaction.

faq.question: Does the amount spent on others matter?
faq.answer: Surprisingly little. Studies show that spending $5 on someone else can produce the same happiness boost as spending $20. The act of giving matters more than the amount. Thoughtful small gifts often outperform expensive impersonal ones.
